source_text: Οὐχ εὗρε δ᾿ ὁ Κέλσος προσωποποιῶν τὸν Ἰουδαῖον τοιαῦτα αὐτῷ περιθεῖναι ἐν τῷ λόγῳ, ὁποῖα οὐκ ἂν αὐτῷ ἀπὸ τῶν νομίμων καὶ προφητικῶν προφέροιτο γραφῶν. μέμφεται γὰρ τὸν Ἰησοῦν τοιαῦτα λέγων περὶ αὐτοῦ· ἀπειλεῖ καὶ λοιδορεῖ κούφως ὁπόταν λέγῃ· „οὐαὶ ὑμῖν“ καὶ „προλέγω ὑμῖν.“ ἐν γὰρ τούτοις ἄντικρυς ὁμολογεῖ ὅτι πεῖσαι ἀδυνατεῖ, ὅπερ οὐκ ἂν θεὸς ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ἄνθρωπος φρόνιμος πάθοι. ὅρα δὲ εἰ μὴ ταῦτα ἄντικρυς ἀναστρέφει ἐπὶ τὸν Ἰουδαῖον. ἀπιλεῖ γὰρ ἐν ταῖς νομικαῖς καὶ προφητικαῖς γραφαῖς ὁ θεὸς καὶ λοιδορεῖ, ὁπόταν λέγῃ, οὐκ ἐλάττονα τῶν ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ „οὐαί·“ ὁποῖά ἐστι τὰ ἐν Ἡσαΐᾳ οὕτως ἔχοντα· „οὐαὶ οἱ συνάπτοντες οἰκίαν πρὸς οἰκίαν, καὶ ἀγρὸν πρὸς ἀγρὸν ἐγγίζοντες“ καὶ „οὐαὶ οἱ ἐγειρόμενοι τὸ πρωῒ καὶ τὸ σίκερα διώκοντες“ καὶ „οὐαὶ οἱ ἐπισπώμενοι τὰς ἁμαρτίας ὡς σχοινίῳ μακρῷ“ καὶ „οὐαὶ οἱ λέγοντες τὸ πονηρὸν καλὸν καὶ τὸ καλὸν πονηρὸν“ καὶ „οὐαὶ οἱ ἰσχύοντες ὑμῶν, οἱ πίνοντες τὸν οἶνον.“ καὶ ἄλλα δ᾿ ἂν εὕροις μυρία. πῶς δ᾿ οὐ παραπλήσια αἷς λέγει ἀπειλαῖς ἐστι τὸ „οὐαὶ ἔθνος ἁμαρτωλὸν, λαὸς πλήρης ἁμαρτιῶν. σπέρμα πονηρὸν, υἱοὶ ἄνομοι“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς; οἷς ἐπιφέρει τηλικαύτας ἀπειλὰς. αἵ εἰσιν οὐκ ἐλάττους ὧν φησι τὸν Ἰησοῦν εἰρηκέναι. ἢ οὐκ ἔστιν ἀπειλὴ καὶ μεγάλη γε ἡ φάσκουσα· „ἡ γῆ ὑμῶν ἔρημος. αἱ πόλεις ὑμῶν πυρίκαυστοι· τὴν χώραν ὑμῶν ἐνώπιον ὑμῶν ἀλλότριοι κατεσθίουσιν αὐτὴν, καὶ ἠρήμωται κατεστραμμένη ὑπὸ λαῶν ἀλλοτρίων“; πῶς δ᾿ οὐ λοιδορίαι καὶ ἐν τῷ Ἰεζεκιήλ εἰσι πρὸς τὸν λαὸν. ἔνθα ὁ κύριός ἐστι λέγων πρὸς τὸν προφήτην· „ἐν μέσῳ σκορπίων σὺ κατοικεῖς“; ἆρ᾿ οὖν, ὦ Κέλσε, συνῃσθημένος πεποίηκας τὸν Ἰουδαῖον λέγοντα περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ὅτι ἀπειλεῖ καὶ λοιδορεῖ κούφως, ὁπόταν λέγῃ· „οὐαὶ ὑμῖν„ καὶ „προλέγω ὑμῖν“; οὐχ ὁρᾷς ὅτι ἅπερ κατηγορῶν λέγει ὁ παρὰ σοὶ Ἰουδαῖος τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ταῦτα ἂν λέγοιτο πρὸς αὐτὸν περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ; ἄντικρυς γὰρ ἐν τοῖς ὁμοίοις εὑρίσκεται ὢν, ὡς οἴεται ὁ Ἰουδαῖος, ἐγκλήμασιν ὁ ἐν τοῖς προφήταις θεὸς ὡς πεῖσαι ἀδυνατῶν. ἔτι δὲ φήσαιμ᾿ ἂν περὶ αὐτῶν τοῖς οἰομένοις τὸν παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖον εὖ ταῦτα τῷ Ἰησοῦ ἐγκαλεῖν ὅτι ἀραὶ πλεῖσται ὅσαι ἀναγεγραμμέναι εἰσὶν ἐν Λευϊτικῷ καὶ Δευτερονομίῳ, περὶ ὧν ὡς ἐὰν ἀπολογήσηται ὁ Ἰουδαῖος παριστάμενος τῇ γραφῇ. ἢ τοιούτως ἢ καὶ ἔτι βέλτιον ἀπολογησόμεθα περὶ τῶν νομιζομένων ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ εἰρῆσθαι λοιδοριῶν καὶ ἀπειλῶν. καὶ περὶ αὐτοῦ δὲ τοῦ Μωϋσέως νόμου ἡμεῖς μᾶλλον δυνησόμεθα ἀπολογήσασθαι, ἅτε συνετώτερον διδαχθέντες ὑπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἀκούειν τῶν νομικῶν γραμμάτων ἤπερ ὁ Ἰουδαῖος. ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ Ἰουδαῖος ἐὰν ἴδῃ τὸ βούλημα τῶν προφητικῶν λόγων, παραστῆναι δυνήσεται τῷ μὴ κούφως ἀπειλεῖν καὶ λοιδορεῖν τὸν θεὸν λέγοντα τὸ „οὐαὶ“ καὶ „προλέγω ὑμῖν,“ καὶ πῶς θεὸς ὑπὲρ ἐπιστροφῆς ἀνθρώπων τὰ ποιαῦτα ἂν λέγοι, ἅπερ οἴεται οὐδὲ φρόνιμον ἄνθρωπον ποιῆσαι ὁ Κέλσος. καὶ Χριστιανοὶ δὲ ἕνα θεὸν γινώσκοντες. τὸν ἐν τοῖς προφήταις καὶ τῷ κυρίῳ, παραστήσουσι τὸ εὔλογον τῶν νομιζομένων ἀπειλῶν καὶ λεγομένων παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ λοιδοριῶν. καὶ ὀλίγα εἰς τὸν τόπον λελέξεται πρὸς τὸν Κέλσον, ἐπαγγελλόμενον καὶ φιλοσοφεῖν καὶ τὰ ἡμέτερα εἰδέναι· ὅτι ἆρα. ὦ οὗτος, ἐὰν μὲν ὁ παρὰ τῷ Ὁμήρῳ Ἑρμῆς λέγῃ τῷ Ὀδυσσεῖ· τίπτ᾿ αὖ, ὦ δύστηνε, δι᾿ ἄκριας ἔρχεαι οἶος; ἀνέχῃ ἀπολογίας, λεγούσης ὅτι ὑπὲρ ἐπιστροφῆς τῷ Ὀδυσσεῖ τοιαῦτα προσδιαλέγεται ὁ Ὁμηρικὸς Ἑρμῆς (ἐπεὶ τὸ κολακεύειν καὶ κεχαρισμένα λέγειν Σειρήνων ἐστὶν, αἷς πάρεστιν ἀμφ᾿ ὀστεόφιν θὶς λεγούσαις· δεῦρ᾿ ἄγ᾿ ἰὼν, πολύαιν᾿ Ὀδυσεῦ, μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν)· ἐὰν δ᾿ οἱ παρ᾿ ἐμοὶ προφῆται καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὑπὲρ ἐπιστροφῆς τῶν ἀκουόντων λέγῃ τὸ οὐαὶ καὶ ἃς νομίζεις λοιδορίας. οὐδὲν οἰκονομεῖται πρὸς τοὺς ἀκούοντας διὰ τῶν τοιούτων λόγων οὐδὲ προσάγει αὐτοῖς ὡς Παιώνιον φάρμακον τὸν τοιοῦτον λόγον; εἰ μὴ ἄρα βούλει τὸν θεὸν ἢ τὸν θείας μετέχοντα φύσεως ἀνθρώποις διαλεγόμενον σκοπεῖν μὲν τὰ τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως καὶ τὰ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν ἑαυτοῦ μηκέτι δ᾿ ἐνορᾶν. τί πρέπει τοῖς οἰκονομουμένοις καὶ ἀγομένοις ἀνθρώποις ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου αὐτοῦ ἐπαγγέλλεσθαι καὶ ἑκάστῳ γε κατὰ τὸ ὑποκείμενον ἦθος διαλέγεσθαι. πῶς δὲ καὶ οὐ γελοῖον τὸ πεῖσαι ἀδυνατεῖν λεγόμενον περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ κοινοποιούμενον οὐ μόνον πρὸς τὸν Ἰουδαῖον. πολλὰ τοιαῦτα ἔχοντα ἐν ταῖς προφητείαις. ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς Ἕλληνας, ἐν οἶς ἕκαστος τῶν μεγάλην δόξαν ἐπὶ σοφίᾳ ἀπενεγκαμένων οὐ δεδύνηται πεῖσαι τοὺς ἐπιβουλεύοντας ἢ τοὺς δικαστὰς ἢ τοὺς κατηγοροῦντας παύσασθαι μὲν τῆς κακίας ὁδεῦσαι δὲ διὰ φιλοσοφίας ἐπ᾿ ἀρετήν;
pass_a_gloss: Not did-find (εὑρίσκω) Celsus, impersonating (προσωποποιέω) the Jew, such things to put-around (περιτίθημι) him in the discourse as would not be brought-against (προφέρω) him from the legal (νόμιμος) and prophetic writings. For he blames (μέμφομαι) Jesus saying such about him: 'he threatens (ἀπειλέω) and reviles (λοιδορέω) lightly (κούφως) whenever he says "woe (οὐαί) to you" and "I foretell (προλέγω) to you"; for in these he openly (ἄντικρυς) confesses (ὁμολογέω) that he is unable (ἀδυνατέω) to persuade (πείθω), which not a god (θεός, anarthrous) but not even a sensible (φρόνιμος) man would suffer (πάσχω).' See whether these do not turn back (ἀναστρέφω) upon the Jew. For in legal and prophetic writings God threatens and reviles, whenever he says, no lesser 'woes' than those in the gospel: such as in Isaiah [5:8, 5:11, 5:18, 5:20, 5:22 quoted]. And you would find countless (μυρία) others. How are not like the threats he speaks of 'woe sinful nation (ἔθνος ἁμαρτωλόν), people full of sins, evil seed (σπέρμα πονηρόν), lawless sons (υἱοὶ ἄνομοι)' and the following [Isaiah 1:4]; to which he adds threats so great, not less than those he says Jesus said. Or is it not a threat, and a great one, the one saying [Isaiah 1:7]? How are there not revilings (λοιδορίαι) also in Ezekiel toward the people, where the Lord (κύριος) is saying to the prophet 'in the midst of scorpions (σκορπίων) you dwell' [Ezekiel 2:6]? Did you then, Celsus, being aware (συναισθάνομαι, pf. ptc.), make the Jew say about Jesus that he threatens and reviles lightly...? Do you not see that what the Jew with you says accusing (κατηγορέω) Jesus could be said to him about God? For plainly in like charges (ἐγκλήματα) is found, as the Jew supposes, the God in the prophets, as unable to persuade. Further I would say to those thinking the Jew in Celsus well charges (ἐγκαλέω) Jesus that very many curses (ἀραί) are written in Leviticus and Deuteronomy; about which as the Jew would defend (ἀπολογέομαι) standing by (παρίσταμαι) the Scripture, either thus or still better we shall defend the revilings and threats thought to be said by Jesus. And about the law of Moses itself we shall be more able to defend, having been taught by Jesus to hear the legal letters (γράμματα) more intelligently (συνετώτερον) than the Jew. But the Jew too, if he sees the intent (βούλημα) of the prophetic words, will be able to support (παρίστημι) that God does not lightly threaten and revile saying 'woe' and 'I foretell to you', and how God would say such things for the conversion (ἐπιστροφή) of men, which Celsus thinks not even a sensible man would do. And Christians knowing one God, the one in the prophets and in the Lord, will show the reasonableness (τὸ εὔλογον) of the supposed threats and the so-called (by Celsus) revilings. A few things on the point will be said to Celsus, professing (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) to philosophise and to know ours: O man, if Hermes in Homer says to Odysseus 'why again, wretch (δύστηνε), do you go over the heights (ἄκριας) alone?', you tolerate (ἀνέχομαι) a defence saying that for conversion Homeric Hermes converses so with Odysseus (since flattering (κολακεύω) and saying pleasing things belongs to the Sirens, beside whom is a heap (θίς) around bones, saying 'come here, much-praised (πολύαινος) Odysseus, great glory (κῦδος) of the Achaeans'); but if the prophets with me and Jesus himself for conversion of the hearers say the woe and what you consider revilings, is nothing managed (οἰκονομέω) toward the hearers through such words, nor does he apply (προσάγω) to them such word as a Paeonian drug (Παιώνιον φάρμακον)? Unless you want God or the one sharing in divine nature (θεία φύσις), conversing with men, to look to the things of his own nature and his own worth (ἀξία), and no longer look into what befits to announce (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) to the men being managed and led by his word (λόγος), and to converse with each according to the underlying character (ὑποκείμενον ἦθος). How is it not laughable, the 'unable to persuade' said about Jesus and made common (κοινοποιέω) not only to the Jew, having many such in the prophecies, but also to Greeks, among whom each of those who carried off great fame for wisdom (σοφία) has not been able to persuade the plotters (ἐπιβουλεύω) or judges or accusers to cease from vice (κακία) and to travel through philosophy to virtue (ἀρετή)?
pass_b_english: Celsus, bringing the Jew on as a speaking character, could find nothing to put into his mouth in his discourse that could not be thrown back at him from the writings of the Law and the Prophets. For he finds fault with Jesus, saying this about him: “He threatens and reviles rashly whenever he says, ‘Woe to you’ (compare Matthew 23:13–29; Luke 6:24–26) and ‘I tell you beforehand.’ For in these words he openly admits that he cannot persuade, which would not happen to a god, nor even to a sensible man.”

But see whether these charges do not plainly turn back on the Jew. For in the writings of the Law and the Prophets God threatens and reviles when he pronounces woes no less than those in the gospel. Such are these words in Isaiah: “Woe to those who join house to house and bring field near to field” (Isaiah 5:8); and “Woe to those who rise early in the morning and pursue strong drink” (Isaiah 5:11); and “Woe to those who drag their sins along as with a long rope” (Isaiah 5:18); and “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20); and “Woe to the strong among you, who drink wine” (Isaiah 5:22). And you could find countless others. And how are the words “Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins, evil seed, lawless sons” (Isaiah 1:4), and what follows, not like the threats he speaks of? These words are followed by threats so great that they are no less than those he says Jesus spoke. Or is it not a threat, and a great one, that says: “Your land is desolate, your cities burned with fire; strangers devour your country in your presence, and it is laid waste, overthrown by foreign peoples” (Isaiah 1:7)? And how are there not insults against the people in Ezekiel as well, where the Lord says to the prophet, “You dwell in the midst of scorpions” (Ezekiel 2:6)?

Did you, then, Celsus, know what you were doing when you made the Jew say of Jesus that “he threatens and reviles rashly whenever he says, ‘Woe to you’ and ‘I tell you beforehand’”? Do you not see that the very things your Jew says in accusing Jesus could be said to him about God? For, by the Jew’s way of thinking, the God of the prophets is plainly found open to like charges, as one unable to persuade.

Further, to those who think that Celsus’s Jew is right to bring these charges against Jesus, I would say this on the point: a great many curses are written in Leviticus and Deuteronomy (see Leviticus 26:14–39; Deuteronomy 27:15–26; Deuteronomy 28:15–68). However the Jew defends them when he stands up for the Scripture, in that way, or even better, we will defend what are taken to be the insults and threats spoken by Jesus. And we shall be better able than the Jew to defend the Law of Moses itself, since we have been taught by Jesus to hear the writings of the Law with more understanding than he does. Yet the Jew too, if he sees the intent of the prophetic words, will be able to show that God does not threaten and revile rashly when he says “Woe” and “I tell you beforehand,” and how God would say such things for the conversion of human beings, things that Celsus thinks not even a sensible man would do. And Christians, who know one God, the same in the prophets and in the Lord, will show the good reason behind what are thought to be threats and what Celsus calls insults.

Let me also say a few words on this point to Celsus, who claims both to be a philosopher and to know our teachings. My good man, if Hermes in Homer says to Odysseus, “Why, unhappy man, do you go once more alone across the hilltops?” (Homer, Odyssey 10.281), you accept the defence that Homer’s Hermes speaks to Odysseus like this to turn him; for flattery and pleasing words belong to the Sirens, beside whom lies “a heap of bones” (Homer, Odyssey 12.45), and who say, “Come here, much-praised Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans” (Homer, Odyssey 12.184). But if my prophets, and Jesus himself, say “Woe” and what you take for insults to turn their hearers, is nothing then wisely arranged for the hearers by such words, and does he not apply such speech to them as a healing remedy of Paeon?

Unless, perhaps, you would have God, or one who shares in the divine nature, when he speaks with human beings, look only to what belongs to his own nature and is worthy of himself, and no longer consider what is fitting to declare to the people who are being guided and led by his word, and to speak with each according to that person’s own character. And how is it not laughable that this inability to persuade should be said of Jesus, when it applies equally not only to the Jew, who has many such things in his prophecies, but also to the Greeks? Among them each of those who won great fame for wisdom was unable to persuade those who plotted against him, or the judges, or the accusers, to cease from wickedness and to travel by way of philosophy toward virtue.

choices.why: κούφως rendered 'rashly' in all three places (was 'lightly', which reads as 'mildly' in English)
'with woes no lighter than those in the gospel' corrected to 'when he pronounces woes no less than those in the gospel' (οὐκ ἐλάττονα; the old wording also clashed with κούφως)
Isaiah 1:4 question reordered so the quoted words are the subject compared with the threats Celsus speaks of (the old order read as if the quotation were Celsus's threats)

choices.term: are we to think that nothing is wisely arranged
choices.why: 'are we to think that nothing is wisely arranged' restored to Origen's direct questions 'is nothing then wisely arranged ... and does he not apply' (the framing 'are we to think' was added)
'what it befits him to declare ... and how to speak with each' corrected to 'what is fitting to declare ... and to speak with each' (two infinitives under one πρέπει; 'how' was added)

rechecked Isaiah 5:8, 5:11, 5:18, 5:20, 5:22, 1:4, 1:7 and Ezekiel 2:6 against the LXX wording; Matthew 23 and Luke 6:24-26 woes; Odyssey 10.281, 12.45, 12.184; speaker frames (Celsus's charge, his Jew, Origen's reply) correct

translator_notes: Celsus’s words (Koetschau’s quoted fragment) taken as running from ‘He threatens’ through ‘nor even to a sensible man’. The anarthrous θεός in the Jew’s mouth is rendered ‘a god’ (generic); Origen then turns the charge onto ὁ θεός of the prophets, rendered ‘God’. ‘Woe to you’ is a clear allusion to the gospel woes (Matthew 23; Luke 6:24–26; also Luke 11:42–52); ‘I tell you beforehand’ (προλέγω ὑμῖν) has no exact gospel match (compare Matthew 24:25, Mark 13:23 προείρηκα; Galatians 5:21 προλέγω), so it is left uncited. Isaiah quotations follow the LXX (5:22 LXX οἱ ἰσχυροὶ ὑμῶν οἱ τὸν οἶνον πίνοντες; Origen’s ἰσχύοντες). Ezekiel 2:6 follows LXX wording. Curses in Leviticus and Deuteronomy are cited to the main curse passages (Leviticus 26:14–39; Deuteronomy 27:15–26; 28:15–68); this is a general reference, not a quotation. Staged text reads ἀπιλεῖ (read ἀπειλεῖ), ποιαῦτα (read τοιαῦτα), and a full stop after γραφῇ that breaks the sentence ‘about which as the Jew would defend ... so we shall defend’; translated as one sentence. Homer: Odyssey 10.281 (Origen’s τίπτ᾿ αὖ for the vulgate πῇ δὴ αὖτ᾿), 12.45, 12.184. Παιώνιον φάρμακον: Paeon is the physician of the gods in Homer. ‘one who shares in the divine nature’ may echo 2 Peter 1:4 (θείας κοινωνοὶ φύσεως) but the wording differs; uncited. ‘One God, the same in the prophets and in the Lord’ may recall Hebrews 1:1–2; uncited. τοῦ λόγου αὐτοῦ (‘his word’) kept lowercase: it may mean his speech or the divine Word; ambiguous. The Greek examples of sages unable to persuade judges and accusers point at Socrates without naming him. Reviewer: λοιδορέω/λοιδορία now rendered consistently as ‘revile’/’insults’ in both Celsus’s charge and Origen’s reply, so the reader sees the charge turned back in the same words. Second reviewer: κούφως rendered ‘rashly’ (thoughtlessly, with levity) wherever Celsus’s charge and Origen’s answer use it.
